questions.prompt: There's an index on (campaign_id, sent_at). A query that filters only on sent_at is slow. Why?
options: The index needs rebuilding.
sent_at is the wrong column type for an index.
Composite indexes are usable left to right — a query that skips the leading column can't seek into it.
MySQL only uses one index per table.
questions.explanation: Think of it as a phone book sorted by surname then first name: searching for everyone called 'Rafi' means reading the whole book. Either add an index leading with sent_at, or reorder the existing one if no query needs campaign_id first. This is the single most common reason an index someone added 'didn't help'.

questions.prompt: Reads go to a replica. Users occasionally don't see a record they created a second ago. What's happening?
options: The write silently failed and the error was swallowed.
Replication lag — the read reached the replica before the write did. Reads that must see your own writes have to go to the primary.
A stale cache in front of the database.
MySQL replication is synchronous, so this isn't possible.
questions.explanation: Read replicas trade consistency for capacity, and the bill comes due exactly here — 'I saved it and it vanished'. The usual fix is routing: after a write, pin that user's reads to the primary for a short window. Chasing it as a cache bug is a day you don't get back.

questions.prompt: Paging through a campaign's messages is fast at first and unusable by page 40,000.

subject.content:
SELECT * FROM messages
WHERE campaign_id = ?
ORDER BY sent_at DESC
LIMIT 50 OFFSET 2000000;

options: ORDER BY ... DESC can't use an index.
LIMIT and OFFSET can't be combined on an indexed column.
SELECT * is the only issue here.
Deep OFFSET makes the server walk and throw away two million rows to return fifty — the cost grows with the page number.
questions.explanation: Keyset pagination fixes it: remember the last row's sent_at and ask for rows older than that, so every page costs the same. It's also more correct — offset paging skips or repeats rows when new messages arrive mid-scroll. SELECT * is a real secondary point on a wide table.

questions.prompt: This archive job has never once finished.
options: One transaction across forty million rows: it holds locks for hours, grows the undo log without bound, and any failure near the end rolls back the entire night's work.
@Transactional belongs on the class, not the method.
findByCampaignId should return a Set to avoid duplicates.
archive.save should be called asynchronously.
questions.explanation: Batch it: chunks of a few thousand, each in its own transaction, with a marker so a restart resumes rather than starts over. Long transactions are the thing that turns a maintenance job into an outage — other writers block behind the locks, and the rollback can take longer than the work did.

questions.prompt: A composite index is defined on (tenant_id, created_at). Which query benefits most directly from its leftmost order?
options: WHERE created_at > ? with no tenant filter
WHERE status = ?
ORDER BY created_at across every tenant
WHERE tenant_id = ? AND created_at BETWEEN ? AND ?
questions.explanation: The index is ordered first by tenant and then by time within each tenant. Equality on the leading column followed by a range on the second lets MySQL scan a narrow contiguous portion of the index.
